title: Regulation, productivity and growth: OECD evidence
venue: Economic Policy 18(36): 9-72 (also OECD ECO WP 347; World Bank PRWP 2944)
method: Industry-level panel regressions of multifactor productivity growth on OECD product market regulation and privatisation indicators, with a catch-up-to-frontier specification
finding: Reforms promoting competition and private governance are associated with faster productivity growth; in manufacturing, liberalisation gains are larger the further a country is from the technology leader, suggesting entry-limiting regulation slows technology adoption. Strict product market regulation and lack of reform appear to underlie the weak productivity of some continental European countries.
summary_plain: Countries that lowered barriers to entering markets saw faster productivity growth, especially where they had most catching up to do. Heavily regulated European economies lagged.
relevance: Seminal source for the claim that rules restricting entry and competition widen the EU-US productivity gap; the DMA aims to raise contestability, but other digital rules may raise entry costs.
caveats: Aggregate regulation indices; associations from panel data with limited exogenous variation; pre-digital era.

authors: Renaud Bourlès; Gilbert Cette; Jimmy Lopez; Jacques Mairesse; Giuseppe Nicoletti
title: Do Product Market Regulations in Upstream Sectors Curb Productivity Growth? Panel Data Evidence for OECD Countries
venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 95(5): 1750-1768 (NBER WP 16520)
method: Endogenous-growth model tested on an industry panel; MFP growth regressed on regulation in supplier (upstream) sectors weighted by input-output links, interacted with distance to frontier
finding: Anticompetitive upstream regulations significantly curbed MFP growth over the preceding fifteen years, more strongly for observations close to the productivity frontier.
summary_plain: When the sectors that supply other businesses (such as telecoms, transport or professional services) are tightly regulated, productivity suffers downstream too, especially for the most advanced firms.
relevance: Digital platforms and cloud/network services are upstream inputs for much of the economy, so the costs or benefits of regulating them spill over to user industries.
caveats: Regulation measured with OECD indices; identification relies on input-output weights and frontier interactions rather than a natural experiment.

authors: Jens Arnold; Giuseppe Nicoletti; Stefano Scarpetta
title: Regulation, Allocative Efficiency and Productivity in OECD Countries: Industry and Firm-Level Evidence
venue: OECD Economics Department Working Papers No. 616
geography_period: OECD countries, harmonised firm-level data, c. 1990s-2000s
method: Industry allocative-efficiency (Olley-Pakes covariance) comparisons and firm-level productivity regressions interacting service regulation with ICT-use intensity and distance to frontier
finding: Resources were allocated less efficiently across firms where service regulation was less market-friendly; anti-competitive service regulation hampered productivity growth in ICT-using sectors, especially for firms catching up to or near the technology frontier.
summary_plain: Tight rules in service sectors made it harder for the best firms to grow and take resources from weaker ones, which slowed productivity in industries that rely on digital technology.
relevance: Directly links regulation to slower ICT-driven productivity in continental Europe, the channel most relevant to digital regulation.
caveats: Working paper; regulation indices are pre-2008 and not specific to digital rules.

authors: Alberto Alesina; Silvia Ardagna; Giuseppe Nicoletti; Fabio Schiantarelli
title: Regulation and Investment
venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 3(4): 791-825 (NBER WP 9560)
geography_period: OECD countries, transport, communications and utilities sectors, 1975-1998
method: Sector-country panel regressions of investment on time-varying OECD regulation indicators (entry barriers, public ownership), with fixed effects and GMM
finding: Various measures of product market regulation, particularly entry barriers, are robustly and negatively related to investment; reforms that liberalise entry are very likely to spur investment.
summary_plain: Sectors where it is harder for new firms to enter invest less; opening them up tends to raise investment.
relevance: Investment in digital infrastructure and AI is central to the EU-US gap; rules that act as entry barriers may depress it, while rules opening gatekept markets may raise it.
caveats: Network industries only; regulation indices coarse; endogeneity of reforms addressed only partly.

title: Macroeconomic Effects of Regulation and Deregulation in Goods and Labor Markets
method: General-equilibrium model with monopolistic competition in goods markets and wage bargaining in labour markets; regulation sets entry costs, competition and worker bargaining power
finding: Deregulation reduces and redistributes rents; even if beneficial in the long run, it can bring incumbent decline, temporarily higher unemployment and lower real wages. Product market deregulation can make labour market deregulation politically easier.
summary_plain: Cutting red tape can raise output and jobs over time, but the gains take time and create winners and losers along the way.
relevance: Frames why regulatory reform in the EU is politically hard and why short-run and long-run effects of digital rules can differ.
caveats: Theoretical; no direct estimate of magnitudes.

authors: Bart van Ark; Mary O'Mahony; Marcel P. Timmer
title: The Productivity Gap between Europe and the United States: Trends and Causes
method: Growth accounting with EU KLEMS industry data decomposing labour productivity into ICT capital, other capital, labour quality and MFP
finding: Since the mid-1990s US labour productivity growth accelerated while Europe's slowed; the gap reflects slower emergence of the knowledge economy in Europe (lower ICT investment contributions, a small ICT-producing sector and slower MFP growth), concentrated in market services, with labour market functioning and high product market regulation as underlying issues.
summary_plain: Europe fell behind the US from the mid-1990s mainly because it used digital technology less productively, especially in services such as retail and finance.
relevance: Establishes that the EU-US gap is largely a digital and services story, the arena of EU digital regulation.
caveats: Accounting decomposition, not causal; regulation named as an underlying factor rather than estimated.

authors: Nicholas Bloom; Raffaella Sadun; John Van Reenen
title: Americans Do IT Better: US Multinationals and the Productivity Miracle
method: Compares US-owned, other multinational and domestic establishments operating under the same European regulations; event study of takeovers by US vs non-US multinationals; links to management practices survey
finding: US multinationals in Europe obtained higher productivity from IT than non-US multinationals, and establishments taken over by US multinationals (but not others) raised the productivity of their IT; the US IT-related productivity advantage is primarily due to tougher 'people management' practices.
summary_plain: American-owned firms in Europe get more out of computers than European firms facing the same rules, mainly because of how they manage people.
relevance: Important counterweight: part of the EU-US digital gap reflects management and organisation rather than regulation per se (though labour rules can shape management practices).
caveats: Mostly UK data; management practices can themselves be shaped by labour regulation.

authors: Dan Andrews; Chiara Criscuolo; Peter N. Gal
title: The Best versus the Rest: The Global Productivity Slowdown, Divergence across Firms and the Role of Public Policy
method: Tracks productivity of global frontier vs laggard firms; regressions of the frontier-laggard gap on sectoral product market reform intensity
finding: Labour productivity at the global frontier grew 2.8% a year in manufacturing in 2001-2013 versus 0.6% for non-frontier firms, with an even wider gap in market services; divergence was stronger in industries where product market reforms were least extensive.
summary_plain: The most productive firms keep pulling ahead while the rest stall, and the gap is widest where markets are less open to competition.
relevance: Digital regulation can help (by opening markets to challengers) or hurt (by raising fixed compliance costs for laggards) technology diffusion.
caveats: Working paper; reform-divergence link is correlational; frontier measures sensitive to Orbis coverage.

title: The future of European competitiveness (Part A: A competitiveness strategy for Europe)
method: Policy diagnosis drawing on macro comparisons, sector studies and stakeholder input
finding: Real disposable income per capita has grown almost twice as much in the US as in the EU since 2000; around 70% of the per capita GDP gap with the US at PPP (which rose from 31% in 2002 to 34%) is explained by lower productivity. The EU has around 100 tech-focused laws and over 270 regulators active in digital networks, and many EU laws take a precautionary ex ante approach that the report says hampers innovation.
summary_plain: The EU's former central bank chief found Europe falling behind the US mainly on productivity and argued that layers of tech regulation and a fragmented single market hold innovators back.
relevance: The most influential recent EU diagnosis directly naming the volume of digital regulation as a drag on innovation.
caveats: Policy report, not peer-reviewed; the 100-laws count is an inventory, not an impact estimate.

title: From laggard to leader? Closing the euro area's technology gap
venue: ECB speech, European University Institute, Florence, 16 February 2024
method: Speech synthesising ECB staff and academic research
finding: Big-four euro area labour productivity rose from 25% of the US level in 1945 to 100% in 1995, then fell back to about 0.8 by 2008; US services productivity grew 3.2% a year in 1995-2005 versus 0.9% in Europe. She cites evidence that strict product market regulation, rigid labour markets and red tape inhibited digital adoption, and that intra-EU services trade is only about 15% of GDP versus over 50% for goods because of remaining regulatory barriers.
summary_plain: A senior ECB official argued that Europe's productivity gap with the US is largely about slow adoption of digital technology, held back by red tape, fragmented markets and weak scale-up finance.
relevance: Central-bank view that fragmentation and entry barriers, rather than regulation as such, are the main issue, favouring harmonised single-market rules.
caveats: Speech; numbers drawn from cited studies, not original estimates. In a February 2026 speech ('Made in Europe') she called the 'over-regulation' narrative misleading while stressing internal barriers and national gold-plating.

authors: International Monetary Fund, European Department (underlying work: Adilbish, Cerdeiro, Duval, Hong, Mazzone, Rotunno, IMF WP 2025/040)
title: Regional Economic Outlook: Europe, October 2024 (and 'Europe's Productivity Weakness: Firm-Level Roots and Remedies', IMF WP/25/40)
venue: IMF Regional Economic Outlook; IMF Working Paper
geography_period: EU vs US states, trade costs for 2020; firm data Europe and US
method: Structural gravity model comparing cross-border with domestic trade flows; residual trade costs converted to ad valorem tariff equivalents
finding: Intra-EU trade costs in 2020 were equivalent to an ad valorem tariff of about 44% for the average manufacturing sector (vs about 15% between US states) and about 110% for services. The working paper finds smaller markets and limited market-based finance are key bottlenecks for Europe's frontier firms.
summary_plain: The IMF estimates that hidden barriers inside the EU's single market, such as differing national rules, raise costs as much as a large tariff would, especially for services.
relevance: Supports the case that EU-level harmonised digital rules can replace 27 national regimes and reduce internal trade costs.
caveats: Residual-based gravity estimate captures all border frictions (language, distance, preferences), not only regulation; critics (e.g. a VoxEU column, Bini Smaghi at Bocconi IEP) argue it is too high and sensitive to data choices; some sources quote 45%.

authors: European Parliamentary Research Service (Joseph Dunne et al.)
title: Europe's two trillion euro dividend: Mapping the Cost of Non-Europe, 2019-24
method: Compilation of sectoral 'cost of non-Europe' estimates of gains from adopting and implementing Parliament-backed EU policies
finding: Potential gains of over EUR 2.2 trillion (about 14% of 2017 EU GDP) if Parliament-backed policies were adopted and fully implemented over 2019-2029, measured mainly as additional GDP.
summary_plain: The European Parliament's research service estimates that completing pending EU-level policies, including the digital single market, could add very large sums to EU output over a decade.
relevance: Common source for the claim that more (harmonised) EU regulation raises GDP, the opposite of the burden narrative.
caveats: Aggregates heterogeneous studies with different methods; produced by an institution that advocates EU action; gains are cumulative over ten years, not annual.

authors: Thierry Mayer; Vincent Vicard; Soledad Zignago
title: The cost of non-Europe, revisited
geography_period: EU member states, gravity data to the 2010s
method: Structural gravity estimation of EU single market trade creation versus ordinary regional trade agreements, then general-equilibrium counterfactuals (shallow RTA or WTO rules, with/without Brexit)
finding: Working-paper version: the Single Market raises bilateral trade more than three times as much as a typical regional trade agreement, and the trade-related cost of non-Europe is about 3% to 7% of GDP on average depending on the counterfactual, largest for small open (especially Eastern) economies.
summary_plain: Deep EU integration, including common rules, has boosted trade among members far more than ordinary trade deals, and undoing it would cost several percent of GDP.
relevance: Evidence that harmonised rules (as opposed to national ones) raise trade and income, relevant to the single-market rationale of EU digital laws.
caveats: Headline numbers confirmed in the working paper, not checked in the journal text; captures all EU integration, not regulation alone.

title: How European Markets Became Free: A Study of Institutional Drift
venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 21(1): 251-292 (NBER WP 24700)
geography_period: EU and US product markets, c. 1995-2015
method: Political-economy model of national vs supranational regulators, tested with cross-country evidence on regulation, regulator independence and competition enforcement
finding: Countries in a single market willingly promote a supranational regulator that enforces free markets beyond any single country's preferences; EU institutions are more independent and enforce competition more strongly than any member state did, with larger benefits for countries with weaker institutions.
summary_plain: Contrary to the image of an over-regulated Europe, EU-level rules and enforcement made many European markets more competitive than US ones.
relevance: Contrary evidence: EU-level regulation (such as competition law and arguably the DMA) can increase competition rather than burden it.
caveats: Focus on competition policy and market regulation, not compliance-heavy rules; the working-paper title claimed EU markets became more competitive than US markets, a broader claim than the published abstract makes.
